title: The 'Tenth Justice': Government's Lawyer at the Court
hook: One lawyer appears in most Supreme Court cases, keeps an office inside the courthouse, and shapes what the Court decides by choosing which questions to put in front of it.
key_points: The Solicitor General, created by Congress in 1870, represents the federal government before the Supreme Court.
The nickname 'tenth justice' reflects the office's unusual access and influence — it even keeps an office at the courthouse.
SCOTUSblog reports the office argues roughly 50 of the 65–70 annual oral arguments and is involved in as much as 90% of the Court's work.
Its real leverage is framing: which issues to appeal, which to separate, and which arguments to lead with.
In the birthright citizenship litigation, Acting SG Sarah Harris split the nationwide-injunction question from the constitutional merits — winning the first while losing the second.
Across two agency-independence cases the office pressed separation-of-powers arguments in one and factual misconduct claims in the other, inviting different outcomes.
content_html: Almost every country's government needs a lawyer for its highest court, but the U.S. version has an unusual amount of gravity. The Solicitor General — an office Congress created in 1870 — represents the federal government at the Supreme Court, and is nicknamed the "tenth justice" for how close it sits to the Court's work. SCOTUSblog's Stephen Wermiel reports the office argues around 50 of the 65–70 oral arguments each year, is involved in as much as 90% of the Court's business, and even keeps an office in the courthouse itself.
extra_html: Wermiel's point is that the office's power is strategic rather than formal: it has no vote, but it decides which cases the government appeals and how the questions get carved up. He offers two examples from recent litigation. In the birthright citizenship fight, Acting Solicitor General Sarah Harris separated the question of nationwide injunctions from the underlying constitutional question — an approach that let the administration win on injunctions while losing on the policy, a split outcome that arguing both together might have made impossible. In two cases about the independence of federal agencies, the office pressed aggressive separation-of-powers arguments in the FTC firing case but leaned on factual misconduct claims in the Federal Reserve case, framing that, in Wermiel's reading, may have let the Court unsettle longstanding precedent in one area while leaving central-bank independence alone. The general civics lesson: in litigation, whoever controls the question often controls the answer. (This card describes the U.S. federal system specifically.)

related.title: Who Are the "Friends of the Court"?
related.hook: Most briefs a supreme court reads are filed by people who aren't suing anyone. The amicus brief is how outside interests get a say in a case they are not party to.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: When Federal Law Means Different Things in Different States
related.hook: Nine federal appeals courts have read the same detention statute; seven say one thing and two say the opposite. Until the Supreme Court steps in, your rights depend on your address.

related.title: Can the President Fire the Heads of Independent Agencies?
related.hook: For 91 years, a 1935 precedent shielded independent agency heads from being fired at a president's will. In 2026 the Supreme Court swept most of that shield away.

flashcards.prompt: Who is the 'tenth justice' and what does the office do?
flashcards.back_html: The Solicitor General — the official who represents the federal government before the Supreme Court. Created by Congress in 1870.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the Solicitor General's greatest influence come from?

choices.text: Choosing which questions to bring and how to frame them
Casting a tie-breaking vote when the justices split evenly
Selecting which justices hear each case

flashcards.explanation_html: The office has no vote. It shapes outcomes by deciding what to appeal, what to separate out, and which arguments to lead with.

flashcards.prompt: In the birthright citizenship litigation, what was the strategic move described?

choices.text: Separating the nationwide-injunction question from the constitutional merits
Asking the Court to skip oral argument entirely
Declining to participate so a private party could argue instead

flashcards.explanation_html: Splitting the issues let the administration win on injunctions while losing the underlying policy question — a partial victory that a combined argument might have foreclosed.
